gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Which?'s lab, testing against a medical-grade chest strap, measured the $99.99 Google Fitbit Air at 1.34% overall heart-rate error against a 5.7% average for fitness trackers, and at 199 hours on one charge against Google's 'up to 7 days' claim. Which? also measured smart rings at an average 20.2% error for resting heart rate, against 2.3% for fitness trackers.
standout_why: I could not open any of the three cited rival pages (womenshealthmag.com, goodhousekeeping.com, wired.com). WebFetch is blocked on all three, the search tool refuses those domains, and shell curl was not approved. The uncited wearablebeat.com page returned 403. So the judgement that they lack these lab figures is untested. It rests on ChatGPT's answer, which built on those pages: it quotes only maker claims ('up to 7 days', 'up to 11 days', 'shorter battery'), has no measured error rates, no measured runtimes and no chest-strap comparison, and recommends a ring for 'sleep, recovery, and cycle insights' without any accuracy figure.
decides: It confirms the Fitbit Air as the budget pick on measured data. Which? found 1.34% heart-rate error, 1.66% walking step error and 199 h of battery, but also 10.8% overall distance error because it has no onboard GPS. It challenges ChatGPT's #1 pick, the Fitbit Charge 6: GearLab gave it a 96.54% heart-rate accuracy score and said it misses rapid changes, while the Fitbit Inspire 3 on our page scored 100%. It backs the vívoactive 6 for running, since OutdoorGearLab measured a 1.0 bpm median difference against a reference sensor and ±0.04 mi on a 2-mile course. It adds a caution to the ring pick: Which? found smart rings averaged 20.2% resting heart-rate error. That is a category average from about 4 rings, not an Oura result. Oura Ring Gen 4 itself scored 98.65% in GearLab's test.

findings.label: Overall heart-rate error (Which? lab)
findings.value: 1.34% (smartwatch avg 3.85%, fitness tracker avg 5.7%, smart ring avg 9.36%)
findings.source_title: Fitbit Air review: is this screenless tracker worth the money? – Which?
findings.note: Which? Product Testing, Adam Speight, published 2026-08-28. Error is measured against a medical-grade chest strap. Resting heart-rate error was 0.83%, against a 20.25% smart-ring average.

findings.label: Battery life on one charge (Which? lab)
findings.value: 199 h (just over 8 days); full charge 1 h 2 min; 30 min of charging restores 67%
findings.source_title: Fitbit Air review: is this screenless tracker worth the money? – Which?
findings.note: Which? standard usage routine, published 2026-08-28. Google claims up to 7 days, so 199 h is about 1.2 times the claim (168 h).

findings.label: Walking step error / overall distance error / running error (Which? lab)
findings.value: 1.66% steps (tracker avg 3.26%); 10.8% distance (tracker avg 10.22%, GPS smartwatch avg 2.98%); 2.35% running (tracker avg 9.22%)
findings.source_title: Fitbit Air review: is this screenless tracker worth the money? – Which?
findings.note: Published 2026-08-28. The Air has no onboard GPS and uses the phone's GPS.

findings.label: Heart-rate error by category and brand (Which? lab)
findings.value: Resting error: fitness trackers 2.3%, smartwatches 3%, smart rings 20.2%. Running error: trackers 9.2%, smartwatches 6%, rings 5.6%. Overall error by brand: Apple 1.1%, Google 1.79%, Garmin 2.5%, Samsung 2.58%
findings.source_title: Which smartwatch brands are most accurate for heart rate? Plus tips to improve tracking – Which?
findings.note: Published 2026-02-03. Compared against a medical-grade chest strap. Samples: over 80 smartwatches, about 15 trackers, about 4 rings; Which? itself says the ring figures are less reliable. These are brand and category averages, not results for specific models. The article's text and table disagree on Google's resting figure (1.03% vs 0.74%). No breakdown by sex, wrist size or skin tone.

findings.label: Measured GPS battery, heart rate vs reference, GPS distance, charge time, weight (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.value: 20 h GPS-only (Garmin claims 21 h); median 1.0 bpm difference after convergence (~15 min); ±0.04 mi on a 2-mile course; 118 min empty to full; 1.3 oz
findings.note: Matthew Richardson, GearLab, 2026-05-22. The heart-rate reference was a Polar Verity Sense armband, not a chest strap. The wrist readings lagged in the first minutes. GPS drifted under heavy tree cover.

findings.label: GearLab 'Measured Heart Rate Accuracy' score
findings.note: Hale Milano with Genaveve Bradshaw, updated 2025-08-13. Compared against a chest-strap monitor. The page does not say how the percentage is calculated.

findings.label: GearLab 'Measured Heart Rate Accuracy' score
findings.note: Updated 2025-08-13. GearLab says it misses rapid changes but is reasonable for averages. Same undefined percentage method as above.

findings.label: Average heart rate on a run vs Polar H10 (Reviewed)
findings.value: 144 bpm vs 148 bpm; within 5 bpm of the H10 average on all 3 runs
findings.note: Christian de Looper, updated 2024-03-07. Three runs; per-run figures were given for one run only.

findings.label: GearLab heart-rate accuracy score and observed battery
findings.value: 98.65%; about 8 days per charge observed; about 20 min to full; 0.2 oz
findings.note: Updated 2025-08-13. Battery comes from long-term wear. The heart-rate percentage method is undefined.

findings.label: GPS track and heart rate vs other watches (DC Rainmaker)
findings.value: No numeric error published; GPS track 'near identical' to Fenix 8 and Apple Watch Ultra 2; heart rate '1-2 minor-ish mistakes' on a trail run
